narrative:
Your predicted probability of leaving is 68%, which means the model sees you as more likely to leave than stay, and that is why the promotion was denied. The strongest signal pushing toward leaving is that you have received other job opportunities while working here. Compared with employees who are predicted to stay, only about one in four have outside offers, so your situation stands out. The model interprets this as a sign that you have alternatives and may be actively considering a move.

Your overall experience of six to ten years also pushes in the same direction. While many stayers have fewer than five years of experience, your longer career history likely makes you more attractive to other employers and more willing to change jobs. Interestingly, your six to ten years in the current organization have the opposite effect. That tenure works in your favor and lowers the leaving risk, because longer service in one place often signals loyalty and deeper roots. However, this protective influence is not enough to outweigh the two factors pointing toward leaving.

Put together, the main story is that you are a valuable employee with outside options and enough experience to act on them. The organization should consider whether it can offer you a compelling reason to stay, such as a real promotion path, more challenging responsibilities, or better recognition. For your part, think about whether the current role still meets your long-term goals. The prediction is not a judgment of your character or performance; it is simply a warning that your departure is likely, and that risk is what led to this difficult decision.
